nameStory: This mushroom's scientific name tells quite a story - 'albocrenulata' means 'white-scalloped,' referring to the distinctive white, wavy edge around its cap. It's been shuffled between several mushroom families over the years, earning it multiple scientific names as mycologists debated where it truly belongs!
description: The White-Scalloped Mushroom is a distinctive orange-capped fungus that grows on decaying wood throughout New England. Its orangish cap can reach up to 3½ inches across, while the stem stretches up to nearly 5 inches tall. What makes it stand out is the characteristic white, wavy edge around the cap rim that gives it its common name. This medium-sized mushroom is a wood-decay specialist, breaking down dead hardwood trees.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Orangish colored cap up to 3½ inches wide with a distinctive white, scalloped or wavy edge - this white rim is the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Sturdy stem up to 5 inches long, typically paler than the cap with a firm, fibrous texture

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Brown spore print - collect spores on white paper by placing the cap gill-side down overnight

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Gills attached to the stem, starting light colored and darkening with age as the brown spores mature

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always found on or very near decaying hardwood logs, stumps, or buried wood - never on the ground away from wood

habitat: Look for this mushroom on decaying hardwood logs, stumps, and fallen branches throughout New England's mixed and deciduous forests. It particularly favors oak, maple, and beech wood in various stages of decay. You'll often find it in moist woodland areas where fallen logs retain moisture, from lowland forests up to mid-elevation slopes.

seasonality.spring: Rarely fruits in spring, but old specimens from fall may occasionally persist in protected spots if winter was mild.
seasonality.summer: Primary fruiting season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of warm rain that penetrate the forest canopy.
seasonality.fall: Peak season continues through fall with fresh flushes appearing after autumn rains, often the best time to find perfect specimens.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting stops with hard frosts, though dried caps may persist on logs as papery remnants until spring.

funFact: This mushroom is such a taxonomic wanderer that it's been classified in four different genera over 150 years - scientists kept moving it around because it looks like a Pholiota mushroom but lacks the golden microscopic structures that define that group!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with orange Pholiota species, but the white scalloped cap edge is unique to this species. Remember: 'White rim wins' - no other orange wood-decay mushroom in New England has that distinctive white, wavy border around the cap.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name shuffle reflects real confusion about where this mushroom belongs in the fungal family tree - it was bounced between Agaricus, Pholiota, Stropharia, and finally Hemistropharia as DNA studies revealed its true relationships.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus Hemistropharia, compare it to its former family Pholiota. Unlike true Pholiota mushrooms, it lacks the golden, crystalline structures called chrysocystidia under the microscope and has notably darker spores. The white cap edge also distinguishes it from any orange Pholiota species you might encounter.
